text:
“I saw that perfectly well,” resumed the canon. “But at this moment you are saying to yourself: This Spanish canon is inventing anecdotes and squeezing history to prove to me that I have been too virtuous...”

Lucien began to smile when he saw his thoughts so accurately divined.

“Well then, young man, let us take facts that have passed into the realm of commonplace,” said the priest. “One day France is almost entirely conquered by the English; the king has only one province left. From the midst of the people two beings arise: a poor young girl, that same Joan of Arc of whom we were speaking; then a burgher named Jacques Cœur. The one gives her arm and the prestige of her virginity, the other gives his gold: the kingdom is saved. But the girl is captured!... The king, who can ransom the girl, lets her be burned alive. As for the heroic burgher, the king allows his courtiers, who make a quarry of him, to accuse him of capital crimes. The spoils of the innocent man, hunted down, surrounded, struck down by justice, enrich five noble houses... And the father of the Archbishop of Bourges leaves the kingdom, never to return, without a penny of his property in France, having no money of his own other than what he had entrusted to the Arabs, to the Saracens in Egypt. You may still say: These examples are very old; all this ingratitude has had three hundred years of Public Education, and the skeletons of that age are fabulous. Well then, young man, do you believe in France’s latest demigod, Napoleon? He kept one of his generals in disgrace; he made him a marshal only reluctantly and never willingly made use of him. That marshal’s name was Kellermann. Do you know why?..... Kellermann saved France and the First Consul at Marengo by a daring charge that was applauded amid blood and fire. That heroic charge was not even mentioned in the bulletin. The cause of Napoleon’s coldness toward Kellermann is also the cause of the disgrace of Fouché, of the Prince de Talleyrand: it is the ingratitude of King Charles VII, of Richelieu, ingratitude...”

“But, Father, supposing you were to save my life and make my fortune,” said Lucien, “you are thus making gratitude easy enough for me.”

“You little rascal,” said the abbé, smiling and taking Lucien by the ear to twist it with an almost royal familiarity, “if you were ungrateful to me, you would then be a strong man, and I would not hold it against you; but you have not reached that point yet, for, a mere schoolboy, you tried to become a master too soon. That is the failing of the French in your time. They have all been spoiled by Napoleon’s example. You resign your commission because you cannot obtain the epaulette you desire... But have you subordinated all your desires, all your actions, to a single idea?...”

“Alas! no,” said Lucien.

“You have been what the English call inconsistent,” resumed the canon with a smile.

“What does it matter what I have been, if I can no longer be anything!” Lucien replied.

“Let there be, behind all your fine qualities, a force semper virens,” said the priest, intent on showing that he knew a little Latin, “and nothing in the world will withstand you. I already love you well enough...”

Lucien smiled incredulously.

“Yes,” resumed the stranger, responding to Lucien’s smile, “you interest me as though you were my son, and I am powerful enough to speak to you with an open heart, as you have just spoken to me. Do you know what pleases me about you?... You have wiped the slate clean within yourself, and you can therefore listen to a course in morality that is taught nowhere; for men, when gathered in a crowd, are even more hypocritical than they are when their interests compel them to play a part. Thus one spends a good part of one’s life weeding out what one allowed to grow in one’s heart during adolescence. That operation is called acquiring experience.”

As he listened to the priest, Lucien was saying to himself: “Here is some old politician delighted to amuse himself on the road. He enjoys making a poor boy whom he finds on the brink of suicide change his mind, and he will drop me at the end of his jest... But he has a fine grasp of paradox, and he seems to me every bit as able as Blondet or Lousteau.”

Despite this judicious reflection, the corruption that this diplomat was attempting upon Lucien was sinking deeply into a soul quite disposed to receive it, and wrought all the greater havoc there because it was supported by famous examples. Captivated by the charm of this cynical conversation, Lucien clung all the more willingly to life because he felt himself being drawn back from the depths of his suicide to the surface by a powerful arm.

In this, the priest was plainly triumphant. And so, from time to time, he had accompanied his historical sarcasms with a mischievous smile.

“If your way of treating morality resembles your way of viewing history,” said Lucien, “I should very much like to know what, at this moment, is the motive behind your apparent charity?”

“That, young man, is the final point of my sermon, and you will allow me to reserve it, for then we shall not part today,” he replied, with the subtlety of a priest who sees his stratagem succeeding.

“Well then, talk to me about morality?” said Lucien, saying to himself: “I am going to make him show himself off.”

“Morality, young man, begins with the law,” said the priest. “If religion alone were at issue, laws would be useless: religious peoples have few laws. Above civil law stands political law. Well then, do you want to know what, for a statesman, is written across the brow of your nineteenth century? In 1793 the French invented popular sovereignty, which ended in an absolute emperor. So much for your national history. As for morals: Madame Tallien and Madame de Beauharnais behaved in the same way; Napoleon married the one, made her your empress, and never consented to receive the other, although she was a princess. A sans-culotte in 1793, Napoleon put on the Iron Crown in 1804. The ferocious devotees of Equality or Death in 1792 became, by 1806, accomplices of an aristocracy legitimized by Louis XVIII. Abroad, the aristocracy that reigns today in its Faubourg Saint-Germain did worse: it practiced usury, kept shop, made little pies, worked as cooks, farmers, and shepherdesses. In France, therefore, in political law as in moral law, one and all have belied their beginnings by their endings, their opinions by their conduct, or their conduct by their opinions. There has been no consistency, either in government or among private individuals. And so you no longer have any morality. Today, among you, success is the supreme justification for every action, whatever it may be. The deed is therefore no longer anything in itself; it lies wholly in the idea others form of it. From this, young man, comes a second precept: keep up a fine appearance! Conceal the reverse side of your life, and display a very brilliant face. Discretion, that motto of the ambitious, is the motto of our Order: make it yours. The great commit almost as many acts of cowardice as the wretched; but they commit them in the shadows and parade their virtues: they remain great. The lowly display their virtues in the shadows and expose their wretchedness in broad daylight: they are despised. You concealed your greatness and allowed your wounds to be seen. You openly had an actress as your mistress; you lived at her home, with her: you were in no way blameworthy, everyone considered both of you perfectly free; but you flew in the face of society’s ideas, and you did not receive the consideration society grants to those who obey it. If you had left Coralie to that Monsieur Camusot, if you had concealed your relations with her, you would have married Madame de Bargeton, you would now be prefect of Angoulême and Marquis de Rubempré. Change your conduct: put your beauty, your graces, your wit, your poetry on display. If you permit yourself petty acts of infamy, let them take place within four walls: then you will no longer be guilty of leaving a stain upon the scenery of that great theater called the world. Napoleon calls that washing one’s dirty linen in the family. From the second precept follows this corollary: everything lies in form. Grasp clearly what I call Form. There are uneducated people who, driven by need, violently take some sum or other from another person: they are called criminals, and they are forced to answer to justice. A poor man of genius discovers a secret whose exploitation is equivalent to a treasure; you lend him three thousand francs—following the example of those Cointets who found your three thousand francs in their hands and are going to strip your brother-in-law—you torment him in such a way as to make him surrender all or part of the secret; you answer only to your conscience, and your conscience does not bring you before the Court of Assizes. The enemies of the social order take advantage of this contrast to yelp at justice and wax indignant in the name of the people because a man who steals chickens by night within an inhabited enclosure is sent to the galleys, while a man who ruins families is imprisoned for scarcely a few months; but those hypocrites know perfectly well that, in condemning the thief, the judges maintain the barrier between rich and poor, the overthrow of which would bring about the end of the social order; whereas the bankrupt, the skillful captor of inheritances, the banker who kills a business for his own profit, merely bring about transfers of fortune. Thus society, my son, is forced to distinguish, on its own account, what I am teaching you to distinguish on yours. The great point is to make oneself equal to the whole of Society. Napoleon, Richelieu, the Medici made themselves equal to their age. You—you value yourself at twelve thousand francs!... Your Society no longer worships the true God, but the Golden Calf! Such is the religion of your Charter, which in politics no longer takes anything but property into account. Is that not saying to all its subjects: Try to become rich!... When, after having known how to obtain a fortune legally, you are rich and Marquis de Rubempré, you will allow yourself the luxury of honor. You will then profess such great delicacy that no one will dare accuse you of ever having lacked it, if indeed you did lack it while making your fortune—which I would never advise you to do,” said the priest, taking Lucien’s hand and patting it. “What, then, must you put into that handsome head?... Only the following theme: Set yourself a dazzling goal and conceal the means by which you attain it, while concealing your progress. You have behaved like a child; be a man, be a hunter, lie in wait, conceal yourself in ambush within Parisian society, wait for prey and for chance, spare neither your person nor what is called dignity; for we all obey something—a vice, a necessity—but observe the supreme law! secrecy.”
